children: By Lila MacLellan
Darren Tipton, CEO of Paris Baguette America, has a theory that leaders tend to "fall to one of two sides."

There are people-centric leaders who are "all about their teams," he told me on a recent call. "They create a great culture, but they find it very difficult to hold people accountable and have those difficult conversations." And there are those who are just the opposite: bosses who don't connect as easily with workers yet feel comfortable calling out problems.

In his decades in the industry, including in senior roles at Au Bon Pain and Le Pain Quotidien, among others, Tipton has found that food businesses attract the first type, he said. That's natural because the job itself is all about connecting, he added, but as Paris Baguette expands, he has emphasized the need to balance both modes.

For readers who aren't familiar with the brand, Paris Baguette sells what you might call European- and Asian-inspired pastries, breads and cakes. So it makes pain au chocolat and delicate tarts, but also strawberry mochi donuts or red bean bread. All of its goods are baked on-site by workers who arrive between midnight and 3 a.m.

The privately-owned company was founded in Korea as a subsidiary of that country's large SPC Group, and its first U.S. franchise opened more than 20 years ago. Lately, I've found Paris Baguettes have been popping up all over. Tipton confirmed this: There are currently more than 330 locations-some 77 of which opened last year alone. This year's new launches will total about 100, and there are another 150 or so on deck for 2027, according to the CEO. The goal is to hit 1,000 cafes in the U.S. and Canada by 2030.

Tipton has stayed vigilant about the conflict-avoidance problem since joining Paris Baguette as chief operating officer eight years ago, a couple of years before he was named CEO, he explained. He learned about the importance of balance while working with Frank Guidara, the former CEO of Au Bon Pain and father of celebrated restaurateur Will Guidara , former co-owner of Manhattan's Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park. Guidara Sr. taught him things during one-to-one meetings but he also led by example, Tipton said, "instilling that ownership mentality."
"He was very motivational, very encouraging, but also would call out something if it was amiss; he wasn't afraid-that was very revealing and very powerful for me as a young leader at that point."
Tipton has become the kind of CEO who will have a conversation "head-on" when it's needed, he said. "And I think people respect that ultimately because they know where they stand."

He monitors reviews and customer sentiment every day, he said. Typically, he leaves his executive team and managers to solve problems, but on rare occasions-when there's a persistent complaint at a shop and "when they are not asking the right questions or giving the right answer"-Tipton said, "I'll step in and ask."
"That's not a common practice, for someone at my level, for the CEO to roll up their sleeves and get down to the front lines," he added, but sometimes it's "critical."
One note: We're off for Labor Day on Monday. Enjoy the weekend and see you back here Tuesday.
Lila MacLellan Editor, CEO Brief
